slides.texte_overlay:
Small things that make you
quietly sophisticated
Know how to order wine without the drama. Ask "What do you like right now?" and pick from there. No fake tasting notes, no pretending. Being curious is more sophisticated than faking expertise.
Write things by hand sometimes. A thank-you card, a note inside a book you lend, a few lines with a birthday gift. In a world of quick texts, a handwritten note feels almost old-world elegant.
Know how to set a table and use the right fork. Work from the outside in, bread on the left, glass on the right. Nobody notices when you get it right. Everyone notices when you don't.
Know a little about art and history. Five minutes a day is enough. Walk into a museum and actually understand why a painting mattered. That kind of knowledge never shows off, it just shows.
slides.texte_sophia: Know a little about art and history. A micro-learning app like the Sophia app gives you five minutes a day of it. Walk into a museum and actually understand why a painting mattered.

slides.texte_overlay: Keep your place ready for guests. Clean glasses, a decent candle, something to offer people. When a friend drops by and you're ready, it says more about you than anything you own.
Learn hello, please and thank you before every trip. Say them even with a terrible accent. The effort gets you better service, warmer smiles, and sometimes the table nobody else could get.
Never rush a meal. Put the fork down between bites, talk, let the evening breathe. Eating like you're late for something is the fastest way to look like you don't belong at the table.
